projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Lynn Maurer was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II and Korean War Veteran Robert Lynn Maurer. Mr. Maurer served in the U.S. Marine Corps. Lynn served in the Pacific Theater during World War II and his highest rank was Corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Maurer's home in Willowick, Ohio, on June 5, 2002. Lynn was 77 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I was born and raised in __ near Altoona. I was raised on a farm and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that where you were living when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: -- yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Near Altoona?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that day?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Oh yes, it was a Sunday morning. I was, I was sitting by the radio with my dad and I was going to say something and he put up his finger like that, he wanted to hear about it, you know. So we didn't even -- I never heard of Pearl Harbor before. So, I went to school one year and I didn't go the next year to high school. So my dad asked me, he said, what are you going to do? And I said, well, I don't know. He said, well, you have to get a job; you can't stay home and do nothing. I said, well, I'll have an answer for you pretty soon. So one evening he came home and said, well, were you out looking for a job today? And I said, yeah. He said, did you find one? I said yeah. He said doing what? And I said in the Marine Corps. I said, you have to sign for me. He's oh -- he said, oh my golly -- and my mother had died when I was ten years old. I was, that was 1940 -- no, '35. And he said, well, I'll sign for you, but he says -- like he said, but I hope you know what you're getting into. And he says, I have some advice for you; keep your eyes and ears open, your mouth shut and do as you're told and stay out of trouble. So, I tried to do exactly that, you know. And I, I think that helped me a lot getting back from two wars, you know, World War II and Korea. So my two buddies and I, we went through boot camp and two of us went overseas together and we got separated in Samoa. The other fellow stayed here for a while. And, so I spent 8 weeks in Samoa on defense, 105's.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Let me see, I sent -- I spent Christmas '42 going through the Panama Canal. Speaking of Panama Canal, I said to my wife a number of years ago, I says you know, I says, I went south through the Panama Canal. I says, now I want to go to Mexico and come North without a sea bag and a pack on my back and an M-1 rifle. So that's what we did. So that was nice, it took the whole day to get through there. So then, well the war was over in '45; I got out in November of '45. Then I joined the Seventh Infantry with __, downtown reserves. We got married June 24, 1950. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before we get to Korea, tell me as much as you can about your World War II experiences. Where did you go after Samoa?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: -- oh, after Samoa I went to New Caledonia. I went there for 13 months on defense. Barrage balloons and 90 millimeter antiaircraft guns, and then I went from there to Guadalcanal and joined the 155 long ton outfit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's a "long ton outfit"?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Artillery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Heavy artillery, the heaviest they had then, you know. And so then we, we hit Guam and came back to Guadalcanal. They had new guns waiting for us, so we retrained and, and then they hit Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you in the invasion of Guam?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yes. Yes. Umhumm.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Early on?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me as much as you can about that, memories of that?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Well, there isn't -- the only thing I can tell you about that is that we landed on yellow beach two, and we moved in quite a distance, you know, to get in range. And so, let me see, we went in Agana; Agana, Guam. So we moved, moved in as far as we could, and well, to make a long story short, we secured that, went back to Guadalcanal, and like I said, they had new guns waiting for us. So we continued to train, and then they got us aboard ship without our guns. So we were suspicious as to what was going on. Nobody would tell us. So, we were out for several days and the word got out that we were floating reserves for Iwo Jima. We were out there aboard ship and to this day, I, I keep teasing the guys that were already on the island that they did such a good job that they didn't need us, and I thanked them, and we went back to Guadalcanal, you know. So we went back to Guadalcanal and then we continued to train, and then we took off again and hit Okinawa. And so the 10th Army, they were in charge of the whole operation -- General Buckner. So as I get it, General Buckner thought most of the Jap's were up at the Northern end. And so -- but he sent the Marines up there. So from the time the reconnaissance was taken until the time we hit, the Jap's moved to the Southern end. So we secured the island in, in about a week and then we moved down to the Southern end near Naha. So I -- to this day I think my closest call from the two wars, was we were bivouacking on the way down and I spread my poncho out on the ground to sleep. And that night something was gigging me in the back. So I said to one of the guys, I says, first thing I'm going to do tomorrow morning is pull up this poncho and get my bayonet out and dig that rock out, you know. So the next morning, I pulled up the poncho and got my bayonet out and started pecking away, and it was a land mine with a dud. It was gigging me in the back all night {laughter}. Boy, that, that, that was really something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's good that you didn't swat at it.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other particularly specific or vivid memories about Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Not really, not really. The section chief, well he was in charge of ammunition -- the bulldozers went down there and bulldozed out gun emplacements for us and there was sort of mud, you know, down in this mine field. Well the Army Engineers thought that they were -- they got all the land mines out of there. But this ammunition Sergeant -- he was walking in front of the guns, checking on ammunition, you know, writing it down you know. We weren't there at the time, and the bulldozer must have pushed a land mine up there, and he tramped on it, and I -- it must have blown him 30 feet in the air. Just blew him out, you know. And so then we moved, after we secured this other end, then we moved back up to the Northern end. And then they sent us out on patrols to mop up any, any Japanese that were straying, you know. I'll never forget, we were out there walking along the road on one patrol and there was about three or four, six by six trucks went by with dead Marines that were just stacked up like cord wood, you know. So then, they dropped the bomb, and I had points -- enough to come home, so I was the first one to come home. And like I said before, I joined the reserves in, I think it was about 1949, in around there. We got married June 24 of '50, and the Korean War broke out the day after we got married. So we went to Colorado on our honeymoon. I came home and I got a new car. We jumped in the car and reported back to Camp Pendleton the day after Labor Day. And so I was out there training artillery for -- over there about a month, and then they shipped us overseas and we -- I went to Wonsan, you know. We more or less secured them, but they were, they were still taking pot shots, you know. So then from there, I moved up to Hamhung. That was -- that was secured. And then we got the word from McArthur that we, we'd all be home by -- for Thanksgiving. So in the mean time, we moved on up to the reservoir. And as we moved up to the reservoir, we didn't know it at the time, but the Chink's were back watching us. And we got up there and we were completely surrounded. So then they were told us we had to start fighting our way back. No matter which -- what direction you went, they were there. So we walked about miles down to Hagaru and I got frost bite. I lost part of, oh half of my big toe and part of my left and froze my hands and feet in general. And they flew me from Hagaru to Japan. And so from Japan, they flew us to Hawaii and we got on a globemaster 'til the next day and flew to California and I was in California for a week. Then they flew me in to Philadelphia Naval Hospital and I was there for nine months in the hospital and was in bed for six months. Then they gave me a retirement discharge in 1951 of August. So that just, just about completes that tour. Jokingly, jokingly, I come out Corporal. It took me two wars to make Corporal. Well, you know, there was no ratings in artillery, you know, it depends what outfit you're in. So jokingly, I, I tell people that I tried to join the -- get in the Vietnam War because I wanted another stripe, you know, and they told me I was too old, so that's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other particularly vivid memories of the reservoir at that campaign?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Well, I, I think it was, I think it was sad the way the Chinese treated our prisoners. Not our prisoners, but our wounded that I know of. They'd, they'd jumped up on the truck and machine gun our wounded, and they, they were just ruthless, you know. I would say when I was over there, I thought a lot of the Japanese, during World War II -- how ruthless they were, you know. And it's, it's a sad thing because you just don't think about a war -- it's a lot of nonsense. Basically, nobody wins, you know, it's just stupidity. But, those Japanese, they were something too. You know I couldn't, I couldn't -- I'd never thought the five years that after World War II when I was over there, that I'd be back in Japan. Cause when, when we went over the second time -- went back to Korea, we landed Kyoto, Japan, I think it was Kyoto. And so this one kid from Seattle, Washington, we were on liberty together and we went in this store, you know, and looked around. And he said, don't, don't you sort of feel funny being here five years after the war? He says, how do we know if they're going to kill us, you know. I says, well, I says, that's, that's the chance you take, I guess. So--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of buddies?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: -- oh yes. I still have -- well I still have one buddy, this one fellow that joined with me, he's still back in Pennsylvania and the other buddy, he, he got out of the service about the time I did, from World War II and he took up flying. He took flying lessons back, back in Pennsylvania and killed himself. So those are the only two there, but -- well, there was another one from Altoona too, that I ran into when I was overseas. Given the subjective, well, being a small world, we were on our way to hit Guam, and so we pulled into, I think it was Marshall Islands; it was secured then. We were on top deck waiting for a movie to start and so we were passing around pictures, you know. So this one Navy Crewman, he was sitting behind me, you know, and he tapped me on the shoulder and he said, hey, let me see that picture. And I showed him this picture, it was a picture of my brother. He says, I know him, he says, my wife and I live in the same apartment; 140th and Lake Shore Boulevard. Isn't that something {laughter}?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, wow {laughter}. Now, you mentioned movies. Did you do anything else when you had a chance for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I only ever saw one USO show over there and that was Bob Crosby, Guadalcanal. That's the only USO show I seen over there. I don't know, maybe it was the wrong place {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you close enough to see anything there?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yep, but you couldn't touch {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Who was the lovely lady that day?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Oh, I don't know, I don't know. A lady was a lady then.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it didn't matter.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah, yeah it was --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about letters from home, do you remember those -- mail?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: - oh yes. Yeah, I, I -- they used to tease me because I, I got so much mail, you know. I says, well if you want mail, you have to write. Well who you write to? I says girls {laughter}; that's what I did. I, I was writing this one girl; she went to Euclid High School and I was out here visiting in 1939 and I met her in 1939; no, not 1939, must be '49 -- '48 - '49. And so when I joined the service -- no, no, I met her before that because I joined the service in '45 -- this must have been '42 or around there. So when I was in boot camp, Parris Island, I started writing to her and I was writing to her the whole time I was overseas. So, I was in New Caledonia at the hospital for, for an operation, and I ran into this buddy that I joined with, that killed himself in an plane crash back home. He was down from Bogainville, he had malaria. So he and I were there at the hospital together for a while, and, and this girl I was writing to, she asked me, do you have any girls that one of your buddies would like to write to? So I said, hey Willard, I says, you want to -- do you want to write to a girl? No, he says, I write to one enough, you know. He says, I can't keep up with them. I said, oh come on. So I, I coaxed him into writing. Yeah, so he started writing, and -- with my wife of today. So we came home and came to Cleveland, and he started dating my wife, you know. So then when he, when he got killed, I started dating her. I came out here to Cleveland and was dating her out here then, you know, she was from Euclid. So we dated for four years and then got married. That's how we met {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't have a steady girl you were writing to during the Second World War?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: No. No, no I didn't. It made it easier that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly. Now you were probably on Okinawa when F.D.R. died, right?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yes. Yes, Truman took over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember much of a reaction to that?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: No, just another day. But what I liked about Truman was he fired from the hip.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you when you heard the news that the bomb had first dropped?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: On Okinawa. After, after the war was over there, we were already -- we were going to hit the coast of Japan, that September or November, you know. But then I was back home again, you know. But that, that would have been a blood bath, I mean it. I'm sure they would have thrown everything at us they had. They were a bunch of jerks.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kind of preparations were you making for the invasion of Japan?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: It was all talk -- it was all under the talking stage then and then everything was just dropped after the -- dropped the bomb.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: A rumor was going around, you know, and I thought to myself, well I says, I was over here this long, I says, I'd hate to go back home without seeing Japan, you know. But I -- but then I had to wait five years and go back there on the way to Korea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Could the guys -- could you comprehend what the bomb was?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: No. No, we didn't know how bad it was. We just heard that they dropped a bomb and that ended the war. Dropped the bombs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah that's right.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I'm trying to imagine what it felt like between the bombs. Did they think the Japanese would keep fighting, after the first one?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I wasn't up on that, I wasn't up on that at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: After the first one fell?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Well you know, as I understand it, after they dropped the first bomb, the Jap's, it, it didn't weaken them that much, you know. But when they dropped the second one, then that really took them. But I often wonder if they had only dropped one if it would have stopped the war. You know they, they were so vicious.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of course, there's been the talk that they should have just demonstrated the bomb out on the ocean somewhere.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah, you know I heard a remark the other day, talking about Memorial Day weekend, they said -- somebody said something about -- oh, they shouldn't have dropped the bomb and all that stuff, and this one fellow says, if they hadn't hit Pearl Harbor they wouldn't have dropped the bomb {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: You know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about the World War II experience, do any other particularly vivid memories come to mind about any of that?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I was more or less dormant for about 30 years after World War II, you know. Even after Korea, you know, but then they got involved in the Marine Corps league, and then we started changing war stories, you know. But I wasn't -- I didn't become gung-ho again until I joined, joined the league and started talking about it again. Now I got all kinds of stuff, you know. I got tapes downstairs of "Return to Tarawa," and you name it, of "Victory at Sea."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, your weren't involved at Tarawa were you?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: No, no, huh-huh. I stopped at -- on the way home we stopped at Guam, Saipan, Tinian, Pearl Harbor -- on the way home. We just stopped there to pick up more, more guys, you know. And then I stopped at Pearl Harbor coming home from Korea too. We landed there and -- see, we got home and I said to my wife, I says, some day, I want you to see Hawaii. So, so we've been there twice since.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: So we took the tour once, which I would highly recommend. But when you fly there and go aboard ship and hit the island from -- by ship, you lose a lot of time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Like if you, you like to spend more time on ship then you would do on an island, you know. And that's fine, but to me, that's a waste.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I did -- 12, 13 years ago, I went to Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah. Now I'd like to go back and see the Missouri there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Me too. Any vivid memories about Korea that you haven't told me?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Walking in my sleep at night, coming down from the reservoir. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how many guys of your unit made it out of there?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I, I couldn't say. I don't, I don't have the facts on that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The casualties there were overwhelming?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Oh yeah. Yeah, you know those, those Chinese, when Chiang Kai-shek got kicked out of China, we were sending -- before, we were sending him lend-lease, you know. And then the communists came in and they, they took all of this stuff. And they were using weapons against us like submachine guns, they could use our ammunition, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I'll think of something after you leave {laughter}. That always happens {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That always happens {laughter}, and I'd say if you come up with some stuff, I'll come back.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I can do that.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: But, that Colonel, he can, he can give you a lot of facts, you know. I mean you know, I wasn't over in Korea that long. I went up to the reservoir there, and then, then they told us to start back down, and we started back down, and then they flew me out, you know. Some of the guys were over there much longer than I was. But I don't, I don't even think I was over there more than three weeks, if that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In Korea?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: When I froze, froze up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. So you got there just in time for the reservoir thing?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah. When I was in the hospital in Philadelphia, this one kid, he was 18 years old, he was in the bed beside me; they cut both of his feet off right above his ankles, from frost bite. Some of them -- one guy, coming along in sick call in the morning you know -- and the doctor would come along and start trimming the black stuff off, you know, fingers and toes would fall on the floor. It was a mess. But you -- once you get frost bite, you got it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it just so bitterly cold, or were you not thoroughly prepared?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: 30's, up in the 30's and below, yeah. Yeah, I wake up one night -- we were coming down from reservoir and we had our parka's on, we had long underwear on, our dress green's, and a parka, you name it, a couple pair of socks. We'd lay down and go to, you know try to sleep you know, you'd wake up and there'd be six inches of snow on top of you. And, and, if the Chinese would have known that, they would have had easy pickings. And I'm sure, I'm sure some guys did get it that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There just wasn't uniforms or equipment that could protect you from that?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: The snow -- the boots weren't -- up to par. We went up there and we weren't prepared for it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else? Do you think you got it?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: I think so. When I -- on our way from Guadalcanal to Okinawa, I volunteered for officer's mess. There were only a couple of officers, you know. There were three -- two black guys who were cooks, you know. And two of us volunteered to be mess duty -- we didn't have to, I mean for the officers -- we didn't have to stand guard duty or anything like that, you know. So I had access to the P.A. system up in the, up in the wheel house or wherever, you know -- or where the officers eat. So I asked this skipper, he was a Lieutenant Commander, I says, do you mind if I play music over the P.A. system? Not at all. During the whole way I played music over the P.A. system. From Guadalcanal to Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you got to pick the tunes?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Yeah. You know, with all -- well back in those days, all the music was basically good, and today, as hard hearing as I am, I can hear a boom box coming down the street. It's, it's, stupid. No, we have a -- the "Chosen Few," they have a national organization every two years we meet. But we aren't going this year, they have it in San Antonio and then, and then the -- we don't think they have that much of a program, you know. No excursions, you know. If you want an excursion, you plan it yourself, you know. Nothing's planned for you, you know. In the First Division reunion, they're going to be in New York City, and I don't think anybody's going to that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Too expensive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Oh, it's outrageous.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: But I, I always wanted to go to San Antonio. But every, every couple months our Ohio group, our local group here, we have luncheons. I think on the 15th we're having a Club Lerego, out there across from the Catholic Seminary there, on Euclid Avenue -- we're going to have it there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, how many are in the Ohio group?

sp.speaker: Robert Lynn Maurer
sp.p: Oh, gosh, I couldn't say. I couldn't say.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
